subject: TSMC beat big. Chip stocks fell anyway.
bodyMarkdown:
If you own a Canadian index fund or a target-date RRSP, the AI trade moved more of your money this week than anything the Bank of Canada will do on October 28. Yesterday I wrote about who might never get paid back for the AI build-out, and Thursday's numbers out of Taiwan are the other half of that argument.

## What TSMC actually reported

TSMC, the Taiwanese company that manufactures the chips Nvidia and AMD design, posted third quarter revenue of about US$46.7 billion on Thursday, up 41.2 per cent from a year ago and 16.2 per cent from the previous quarter. That beat its own guidance range of $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion. High performance computing, the segment where AI accelerators live, came in at 68 per cent of revenue and grew 22 per cent in a single quarter. For the fourth quarter the company guided to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, and it held its 2026 **capex** budget (the money it spends building new fabs and buying equipment, as opposed to running them) at US$60 billion to $64 billion after spending $13.8 billion in the quarter. Chief executive C.C. Wei said demand is still far above what TSMC can supply.

## The market sold it anyway

CNBC reported on Thursday that the 20 most valuable AI and semiconductor stocks in the world have shed more than US$1 trillion in value so far this week. Wednesday was the ugly session: the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.88 per cent to 26,692.87 and the S&P 500 lost 1.11 per cent to 7,718.94. TSMC's own shares closed down 1.80 per cent at $422.25 on the day it announced record profit. What people pointed at was the **gross margin** (what is left of each dollar of sales after the cost of making the product), which slipped to 66.4 per cent from 67.7 per cent in the second quarter, with fourth quarter guidance of 65 to 67 per cent. Thursday brought a partial rebound, with the Dow up 1.1 per cent as the 30 year Treasury yield fell 10 basis points to 5.43 per cent.

## The part I keep rereading

ASML, the Dutch company with a near monopoly on the machines that print the finest features on a chip, reported on Wednesday. Quarterly sales came in at 11.7 billion euros, with net income of 5.0 billion euros. It shipped 121 lithography systems in the quarter, against 91 in the second. Management also said that its supply as currently planned for 2027 and 2028 "will not fully meet the demand of our customers." Two companies at the very bottom of the stack, both saying they cannot build fast enough, two years out. Competition is showing up in the numbers too. IDC data reported by Reuters on Tuesday put Nvidia at 34 per cent of China's data centre AI accelerator market in the first half of 2026, on 678,000 units shipped, down 44 per cent from a year earlier. Huawei shipped 572,000 and took 28 per cent, up from a bit over 300,000.

## The takeaway

I am watching the margin line from here rather than the revenue line, because 41 per cent growth is already in the price and a business at 66.4 per cent is not the business investors paid for at 67.7. Closer to home, Statistics Canada said on October 9 that employment fell by 68,000 in September and the unemployment rate rose to 6.5 per cent, which will shape a job in Richmond Hill far more than anything happening in Hsinchu. Canada's September inflation reading lands Monday, and the Bank of Canada decides on October 28 with its policy rate sitting at 2.25 per cent. If you read one Canadian number today, make it the Canadian Real Estate Association's September home sales, out this morning.
